title: India Just Approved Its Biggest Emergency Oil Stockpile in a Decade. The Hormuz Blockade Made the Case.
excerpt: ONGC will build a 1.75 million tonne underground crude reserve at Mangalore — expanding India's emergency buffer by a third — after the Strait of Hormuz crisis exposed how little fuel the country can store.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's emergency oil stockpile expands by 1.75 million tonnes, increasing capacity by nearly a third.
  • Current reserves cover only 9-10 days of demand, far below global standards.
  • ONGC's Mangalore project is part of a broader strategy to enhance India's oil security.
  • India's foreign exchange reserves have decreased to approximately $667 billion amid rising oil vulnerabilities.
  • The Hormuz blockade highlighted India's urgent need for increased strategic petroleum reserves.

When Iran sealed the Strait of Hormuz in late February, India had nine and a half days of emergency crude oil in underground caverns. Not nine and a half weeks. Not nine and a half months. Days. That arithmetic has now produced the largest single expansion of India's strategic petroleum reserves in a decade. Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC), India's top state-owned explorer, announced late Thursday that its board has approved the construction of a 1.75 million metric tonne underground crude reserve at Mangalore in Karnataka — a facility that will expand the country's emergency buffer by nearly a third. The project, which ONGC described as a "project of national importance," marks the first time the company will independently finance the construction of a strategic crude oil storage facility. It will also seek the central government's permission for commercial use of the storage, allowing the reserve to generate revenue when it is not needed for emergencies. ## What India Has Now — and Why It Is Not Enough India currently stores 5.33 million metric tonnes of crude in underground rock caverns at three sites in southern India: Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh, and Mangalore and Padur in Karnataka. These are managed by Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd (ISPRL), a government-owned special purpose vehicle. > **"The project, which ONGC described as a "project of national importance," marks the first time the company will independently finance the construction of a strategic crude oil storage facility."** At current consumption rates, that stockpile covers roughly nine to ten days of demand. The United States, by comparison, holds reserves sufficient for about 40 days. China's strategic reserves are estimated at 80–90 days. Japan maintains about 130 days of emergency supply. India is the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer, purchasing more than 88% of its crude from overseas. The gap between its import dependence and its storage capacity is, by any measure, dangerous. The Hormuz crisis made the danger real. When Iran began interdicting vessels in the strait — through which roughly 20% of the world's oil and LNG flows — India lost access to a significant share of its LPG imports almost overnight. Nearly 60% of India's cooking gas had been supplied from West Asia. Production was emergency-ramped from 35,000 to 54,000 metric tonnes a day. Refineries that had never made cooking gas were reconfigured within days. The government imposed rationing limits to prevent hoarding. The system held. But the message was unmistakable: India cannot afford to be caught this thin again. ## The Mangalore Play Mangalore was chosen for the expansion because the infrastructure is already there. ONGC's subsidiary, Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL), operates a 300,000 barrel-per-day refinery in the city. Half of the existing 1.5 million tonne Mangalore reserve is already leased to MRPL. The other half is leased to Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), reflecting a partnership model that allows the reserve to earn commercial returns while remaining available for strategic drawdown during emergencies. During Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to the UAE earlier this year, ADNOC announced plans to increase its crude oil storage in India to up to 30 million barrels. It also said the UAE would explore storing Indian crude at Fujairah — a port that sits outside the Strait of Hormuz, making it accessible even during a blockade. The new 1.75 million tonne facility will bring India's total strategic storage capacity to just over 7 million tonnes — roughly 51 million barrels, enough for about 12–13 days of demand. It is a meaningful improvement, but still far short of the International Energy Agency's recommendation that member countries maintain 90 days of net oil import cover.

## The Bigger Pipeline ONGC's Mangalore expansion is only one piece of a broader build-out. The government has approved two additional projects: a 4 million tonne reserve at Chandikhol in Odisha and a 2.5 million tonne expansion at Padur. Together with the existing facilities and the new Mangalore extension, these would bring India's total strategic storage capacity to approximately 13.6 million tonnes — enough for roughly 24–25 days of import cover. The investment is substantial. OilPrice.com, citing government estimates, put the cost of the ONGC Mangalore project alone at approximately $1.6 billion. ONGC has not disclosed a timeline, but the urgency of the Hormuz crisis is likely to accelerate approvals. ## What This Means for the Diaspora For Indian Americans and NRIs watching from abroad, India's oil vulnerability is not abstract. It determines the price of cooking gas their parents pay in Bangalore. It determines whether fuel price hikes trigger the kind of inflation that erodes the value of remittances. It determines whether a future crisis in the Gulf — where nine million Indians live and work — spirals into a full-blown economic emergency at home. India's foreign exchange reserves stand at approximately $667 billion, down from a peak of $728 billion in the week the conflict began. The economy grew at 7.8% last quarter. The fiscal cushion exists. The question has always been whether India would spend it on preparedness before the next crisis, rather than scrambling during one. This time, the answer is yes. *Sources: Reuters, Outlook Business, OilPrice.com, Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd, ONGC stock exchange filing*
